title: Dispersed Urban Expansion Amplifies Land Surface Evapotranspiration Loss
content:
Abstract

The expansion of impervious surfaces (IS) substantially modifies urban water cycles and local climate regimes by suppressing evapotranspiration (ET), thereby affecting the sustainability of human settlements. However, most existing studies have emphasized the effects of IS quantity or coverage, while it remains unclear how different spatial patterns of urban expansion—dispersed versus compact—differentially regulate ET loss, as well as the extent of their respective impacts. This study integrates machine learning, interpretable artificial intelligence, and landscape pattern analysis to disentangle, with 256 cities in China as the research area, for the first time, the role of IS spatial expansion mode in regulating ET. Our results reveal that the suppressive effect of IS on ET weakens progressively from humid to arid regions and that its contribution to ET reduction follows a logarithmic growth pattern (all R 2 > 0.6), intensifying most rapidly during initial urbanization. This early-stage sensitivity makes the initial choice of spatial expansion modes critical. Our causal analysis confirms that leap-frogging expansion—characterized by high dispersion and low connectivity—exerts the strongest per-unit-area suppression, reducing ET by 93.1 ± 48.4% more than compact, interior-filling expansion. In humid coastal megacities, each 10% increase in impervious surface percentage under this dispersed pattern reduces ET by 28.2 mm/yr. These findings underscore the critical role played by the spatial pattern of urban expansion in hydroclimatic regulation and provide a quantitative basis for designing climate-resilient cities that sustain both development and ecological functions.
